### Installing a Linux Server

 |

From massive mainframe systems to simple Internet of Things (IoT) devices, smart TVs, phones, and Tera-Core servers—if you can imagine it, it’s probably possible to get a Linux distribution on any given target platform or hardware of your choice. There are many ways to install the software too: via a USB/flash drive, optical media, network, and so on. Network installation options can be a wonderful help when you’re installing a large number of hosts. Another popular method of installing a Linux distribution is from what is known as “Live Media,” which simply allows you to try the software before committing to installing it.

For the purposes of this Linux server installation chapter, keep in mind that there is nothing particularly special about server class installations, except for the salient fact that servers very often perform very specialized functions and are usually dedicated to performing only a suite of specific tasks. As a result, you should avoid installing extraneous software and running irrelevant services on servers because it creates server bloat and can be a drag on system performance.

In this chapter, we discuss the installation process as it pertains to servers and their dedicated functions. We start off with some general server housekeeping considerations.

### Hardware and Environmental Considerations

As you would with any operating system, before you get started with the installation process, you should determine what hardware configurations will work. Most mainstream Linux distros have a hardware compatibility list (HCL) of some sort available on their web site. For example, openSUSE’s HCL database can be found at [http://en.opensuse.org/Hardware](http://en.opensuse.org/Hardware), Ubuntu’s HCL can be found at [https://wiki.ubuntu.com/HardwareSupport](https://wiki.ubuntu.com/HardwareSupport), and a more generic (and older) HCL for most Linux flavors can be found at [www.tldp.org/HOWTO/Hardware-HOWTO](http://www.tldp.org/HOWTO/Hardware-HOWTO).

These sites provide a good starting reference point when you are in doubt concerning a particular piece of hardware. However, keep in mind that new Linux device drivers are being churned out on a daily basis around the world, and no single site can keep up with the pace of development in the open source community. In general, most popular Intel-based, AMD-based, and ARM-based configurations work without difficulty. The same goes for the emerging IoT and open hardware sectors.

A general rule that applies to all operating systems is to avoid bleeding-edge hardware and software configurations in production environments. Although their specs might appear impressive, they may not yet have been through the maturing process that some of the slightly older hardware has undergone. For servers, this usually isn’t too much of an issue, since there is no need for a server to have the latest and greatest toys, such as fancy video cards and sound cards. Your main goal, after all, is to provide a stable and highly available server for your users.

### Server Design

By definition, well-oiled server-grade systems exhibit three important characteristics: stability, availability, and performance. These three factors are usually improved through the purchase of more and better hardware, which is unfortunate. You needn’t always have to shell out thousands of dollars extra to get a system capable of excelling in all three areas—especially when you could have extracted the desired level of performance out of existing hardware with a little tuning. With Linux, this is not difficult; even better, the gains are outstanding!

One of the most significant design decisions you must make when managing a server may not even be technical, but administrative. You must design servers to be *unfriendly* to casual users. This means no cute multimedia tools, no sound card support, and no fancy web browsers (when at all possible). In fact, casual use of a server should be strictly prohibited as a rule.

**NOTE**  Due to the specialized workloads of servers, you will find that servers often have slightly different configurations and design variables. For example, a server dedicated to handling logging information sent to it over the network is going to have especially large partitions set up for the appropriate logging directories compared to a file server that performs no logging of its own.

Another important consideration in planning a server deployment is making sure that it resides in the most appropriate environment. As a system administrator, you must ensure the physical safety of your servers by keeping them in a separate room under lock and key (or the equivalent). The only access to the servers for non-administrative personnel should be through the network. The server room itself should be well ventilated and kept cool. The wrong environment is an accident waiting to happen.

Once the system is in a safe place, planning for emergency power (battery backup) is also crucial—to keep systems running during power failures or other voltage anomalies.

Here are some specific things you can do to improve your server performance:

•   Take advantage of the fact that the graphical user interface (GUI) is uncoupled from the core operating system, and avoid starting the graphical subsystem unless someone needs to sit at the console to run applications. After all, like any other application, the graphical stack uses memory and CPU time, both of which are better off going to the more essential server processes instead.

•   Determine what functions the server is to perform, and disable all other unrelated functions. Not only are unused functions a waste of memory and CPU time, but they are just another issue you need to deal with on the security front.

•   Unlike some other operating systems, Linux allows you to pick and choose the features you want in the kernel. (You’ll learn about this in [Chapter 10](#ch10.xhtml_ch10).) The default kernel will already be reasonably well tuned, so you won’t have to worry about it. But if you do need to change a feature or upgrade the kernel, be picky about what you add. Make sure you really need a feature before adding it.

#### Uptime

All of this chatter about taking care of servers and making sure silly things don’t cause them to crash stems from a longtime UNIX philosophy: *Uptime is good. More uptime is better.*

The Linux/UNIX **uptime** command tells the user how long the system has been running since its last boot, how many users are currently logged in, and how much load the system is experiencing. The last two metrics are useful measures that are necessary for day-to-day system health and long-term planning. For example, if the server load has been staying abnormally and consistently high, it might mean that it’s time to invest in a faster/bigger/better server.

But the all-important number is how long the server has been running since its last reboot. Long uptime is regarded as a sign of proper care, maintenance, and, from a practical standpoint, system stability. You’ll often find Linux administrators boasting about their server’s uptime the way you hear car buffs boast about horsepower. This is also why you’ll hear Linux administrators cursing at system changes (regardless of operating system) that require a reboot to take effect!

### Methods of Installation

With the improved connectivity and speed of both local area networks (LANs) and Internet connections, it is becoming an increasingly popular option to perform installations over the network rather than using local media (optical CD/DVD-ROM, flash drive, and so on).

Depending on the particular Linux distribution and the network infrastructure already in place, you can design network-based installations around several protocols, including the following popular ones:

•   **FTP (File Transfer Protocol)**   This is one of the earliest methods for performing network installations.

•   **HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol)**   The installation tree is served from a web server.

•   **NFS (Network File System)**   The distribution tree is shared/exported on an NFS server.

•   **SMB (Server Message Block)**   In supported distros, the installation tree can be shared on a Samba server or even shared from a Windows box.

•   **PXE, DHCP, TFTP, and IPMI**   These protocols and technologies can be chained together in various ways to seamlessly bootstrap OS installations and provision new servers. The company (Canonical) behind the Ubuntu distro’s Metal as a Service (MaaS) project is a good example of a comprehensive solution that leverages these technologies.

The other, more typical method of installation is through the use of a media image provided by the vendor. This installer image can come in formats such as ISO9660, UDF, IMG, Compressed Raw Disk images, and so on.

Alongside downloadable installer images, some commercial Linux distributions also have options of physical/boxed installation media that can be ordered from them.

Another variant of installing Linux is installing via what is referred to as a “live operating system or live distro” environment. This environment can be a live USB or even a live CD/DVD. The word *Live* here, simply means that the same install medium can be used to boot and try out (test drive) the distribution first *without* actually installing anything onto the drive. It allows the user to have a rough idea of how hardware and other peripherals on the target system will behave. Keep in mind that even when things don’t work perfectly during your tests in a live distro environment, you can usually get troublesome hardware working after the fact with a little tweak here and there—though your mileage will vary.

We will be performing a server class install in this chapter using an operating system image that was downloaded from the distribution web site.

### Installing Fedora

In this section, we will install a 64-bit rawhide version of the Fedora distribution on a stand-alone system. Later chapters build on the groundwork done in this chapter by exploring as well as adding and configuring new subsystems.

**NOTE**  The term *rawhide* refers to the very latest development version of Fedora. This version almost always points to the next release of Fedora. The Fedora Linux distribution is known to be the breeding ground for bleeding-edge, fast-changing, and experimental FOSS technologies—and for this reason it is highly discouraged to use standard/regular Fedora in production environments. The rawhide stream of Fedora is even *much more* experimental and unstable than regular Fedora! We thought long and hard before settling on the rawhide stream of Fedora to use as a our sample server, and we feel it is worth the risk to showcase the very latest FOSS technologies to our readers. Later on, we install the more conservative and stable Ubuntu LTS distro as the other demo distro. But don’t worry if you choose to install a different version or architecture of Fedora. The installation steps involved between versions are similar. You’ll also be fine if you choose to install a Linux distro other than Fedora; luckily, most of the concepts carry over among the various distributions. Some installers are just prettier than others!

#### Project Prerequisites

First, you need to download the ISO for Fedora that we will be installing. Fedora’s project web page has a listing of several mirrors located all over the world. Whenever possible, you should choose the mirror geographically closest to you. The list of official mirrors can be found at [http://mirrors.fedoraproject.org](http://mirrors.fedoraproject.org).

The latest ISO image for the rawhide version of Fedora that we will be using for this installation can be downloaded from the following top-level directory:

[http://download.fedoraproject.org/pub/fedora/linux/development/rawhide/Server/x86_64/iso/](http://download.fedoraproject.org/pub/fedora/linux/development/rawhide/Server/x86_64/iso/)

You can alternatively download the image from this mirror:

[http://mirrors.kernel.org/fedora/development/rawhide/Server/x86_64/iso/](http://mirrors.kernel.org/fedora/development/rawhide/Server/x86_64/iso/)

Once you are at the top level of the web server folder, you will be presented with various downloadable files representing other variants of Fedora rawhide, the upload date, and the approximate file size. For example, you will see files with names like:

Fedora-Server-dvd-x86_64-Rawhide-<DATE-STAMP>.n.1.iso

Fedora-Server-netinst-x86_64-Rawhide-<DATE-STAMP>.n.0.iso>

The files often have the latest upload date stamp (DATE-STAMP) as part of the filename in the form YYYYMMDD, where YYYY is the year, MM is the month, and DD is the day.

**NOTE**  Linux distributions are often packaged by the architecture on which they were compiled to run. You would often find ISO images (and other software) named to reflect an architecture type. Examples of the architecture types are x86/i386, x86_64, and aarch64, where the x86_64 family refers to the 64-bit platforms (such as Phenom, EM64T, Ryzen, and Intel Core i5, i7, and i9).

The next step is to write the ISO image file to a suitable medium.

If you plan on performing the installation using external flash-based media, such as a USB stick, a Secure Digital (SD) card, or an external hard disk, the system needs to be able to boot off the medium. [Appendix A](../Text/app1.xhtml) discusses how to create a Linux installer on flash-based media.

**NOTE**  On the off chance that you have a physical CD/DVD drive on your chosen hardware and blank optical CD/DVD-ROM media, you might want to perform the Fedora Installation using the same, by burning the installer image to the media using your favorite CD/DVD-burning program. Just remember that the file you downloaded is already an exact image of the installer and so should be treated as such. Most CD/DVD-burning programs have an option to create a CD or DVD from an ISO image. Note that if you burn the file you downloaded as you would a regular data file, you will end up with a single file on the root of your optical media. This is *not* what you want.

### The Installation

Let’s begin the installation process.

Insert and boot off the installation medium (optical disk, USB flash drive, and so on). The system’s Unified Extensible Firmware Interface (UEFI) or Basic Input/Output System (BIOS) should be preconfigured to boot from the correct medium. This will present a welcome splash screen, as shown next.

![Images](Images/f0020-01.jpg)

If you do not press any key, the prompt will begin a countdown, after which the installation process will start by booting the highlighted Test This Media & Install Fedora ... option. You can also press ENTER to start the process immediately.

A quick media verification step will take place. This media verification step can save you the trouble of starting the installation only to find out halfway through that the installer will abort because of bad installation media.

After the media check runs to completion, and the media is successfully verified to be usable, the installer will automatically continue to the next screen.

Select the language you want to use to perform the installation in this screen. For this example, we select English (United States). Then click the Continue button.

If you are installing the rawhide version of Fedora, you might see a screen pop up warning you that you are about to install prerelease/non-production software. Click “I want to proceed” to continue.

### Installation Summary

The Installation Summary screen is an all-in-one area where you make the important decisions about the operating system to be installed. The screen is roughly divided into the following sections:

•   Localization (Keyboard, Language Support, and Time & Date)

•   Software (Installation Source and Software Selection)

•   System (Installation Destination and Network & Hostname)

We delve into each of these sections next and make changes where necessary.

#### Localization Section

As the name implies, this section is used for customizing items related to the locale of the system. This includes Keyboard, Language Support, and Time and Date.

##### Keyboard

From the Installation Summary screen, click the Keyboard option to specify the keyboard layout of the system. You can add additional keyboard layouts if you need to in the ensuing screen and specify their order.

For this example, we accept the default value (English US) and make no change. Click Done when you’re satisfied with any changes you may have made here.

##### Language Support

Clicking the Language Support option on the Installation Summary screen enables you to specify support for additional languages that you may need on the finished system.

For this example, we accept the default value (English – United States) and make no change. Click Done when you’re satisfied with any changes you may have made here.

##### Time & Date

Click the Time & Date option on the main Installation Summary screen to bring up another screen that will allow you to select the time zone in which the machine is located. Scroll through the list of regions and cities and select the area closest to you. You can also use the interactive map to select a specific city (marked by a colored dot) to set your time zone.

Depending on your installation source, the Network Time option could be set to ON or OFF by default. Accept the default ON setting; this allows the system to automatically set the correct time using the Network Time Protocol (NTP). Click Done when you’re satisfied with your changes.

#### Software Section

Under the Software section of the Installation Summary screen, you can select the installation source as well as additional packages (applications) that get installed.

##### Installation Source

Since we are performing our installation using a full Fedora image, you will notice that Local Media is automatically specified under the Installation Source section of the main Installation Summary screen.

Clicking on Installation Source will reveal a screen that allows you to specify custom installation sources and additional repositories from which to retrieve installation packages via different network protocols, such as HTTP, HTTPS, FTP, and NFS. This is also where you can specify that the installer download and automatically install the latest packages available upstream—during the installation.

**NOTE**  If you are performing an installation using a minimal Fedora network image that is designed to automatically download the required software from a network source, you will notice that the Closest Mirror option is selected by default for you as the installation source. The Closest Mirror option will automatically determine which country or locale your target system is connected from and use your public IP address to pick a network mirror that is geographically closest to you. This helps to speed up the installation procedure by downloading the needed packages from servers that are closest to you. A sample minimal Fedora network image can be downloaded from here: [https://dl.fedoraproject.org/pub/fedora/linux/development/rawhide/Server/x86_64/iso/](https://dl.fedoraproject.org/pub/fedora/linux/development/rawhide/Server/x86_64/iso/)

##### Software Selection

Clicking the Software Selection option on the main Installation Summary screen presents you with the section of the installation where you can pick the exact software packages that get installed on the system.

The Fedora installer determines which packages are available based on the Fedora *spin* (or edition) that you start off with. Some sample Fedora spins are Workstation, Server, Cloud, KDE, XFCE, and Container. Each spin in turn has several predefined add-ons that comprise software package groups that provide a specific functionality. Sample functionality provided by package groups or add-ons are Basic Web Server, Container Management, Development Tools, Mail Server, Domain Membership, and Editors. Selecting any of the add-ons in the right pane will automatically select/install the actual individual software packages needed to provide the functionality. This organization allows you to select the functionality that you want installed and safely ignore the details.

Here we are using the Fedora Server Edition and thus we have certain predefined add-ons or package groups available to select from, if needed.

Accept the default setting and click Done at the top of the screen.

**CAUTION**  Ideally, on a production system that is supposed to be used as a server for a specific function, you should seriously consider *not* installing any extraneous functionalities or add-ons beyond what is needed to provide the server’s core functions. You should always aim to keep your server as lean as possible. Less is more!

#### System Section

The System section of the Installation Summary screen is used for customizing and making changes to the underlying hardware of the target system. This is where you create your hard drive partitions or volumes, specify the file system to be used, and specify the network configuration.

##### Installation Destination

From the Installation Summary screen, click the Installation Destination option. This takes you to the corresponding task area. This portion of the installation is probably the part that most new Linux users find the most awkward because of the different hardware naming conventions Linux uses. This needn’t be a problem, however—all it takes is a slight shift in thinking. To help with this, keep in mind that *a disk is a disk is a disk* in Linux, Windows, BSD, and macOS.

You will see a screen displaying all the candidate disk drives that you have available on the target system. If you have only one disk drive on the system, as on our sample system, you will see the drive listed under Local Standard Disks with a check mark beside it. Clicking the disk icon will toggle on or off the disk selection check mark. We want it selected/checked here.

The other configurable option in this area is to configure other specialized and network disks such as SAN devices, iSCSI, FCoE, and so on. We are installing on a traditional disk storage device in our example, so we will not be adding any specialized or network disks.

Under the Storage Configuration Options section, select the Custom radio button. Then click Done at the top of the screen.

Once the installer determines that you have a usable disk, you will be presented with the Manual Partitioning screen, shown in [Figure 2-1](#ch2.xhtml_ch2fig1).

![Images](Images/F02-01.jpg)

**Figure 2-1**   Manual Partitioning screen

**NOTE**  If you are performing the installation on a disk with existing data, you can select the “I would like to make additional space available” option under the Storage Configuration area. This will allow the installer to present you with other options to resize or remove existing volumes or file systems on the disk in order to create space for the new OS.

On the Manual Partitioning screen, make sure that LVM is selected as the partitioning scheme for new mount points. LVM is introduced in the following section.

Before we delve into the partitioning setup proper, we will provide a quick overview of the common partitioning scheme and file system layouts.

**Manual Storage Configuration Overview**   Note that even though we selected the custom partitioning option, we are still going to let the installer automatically slice up and lay out the disk for us. We choose this path just so that we can introduce some basic Linux server partitioning concepts. Doing this also gives us a chance to see the structure being automatically created for us—before it is finalized.

The installer provides the option to lay out the disk partition automatically; we will accept the default suggested layout.

**Partitioning Schemes and File System Layouts**

Let’s digress a bit from the actual OS installation and do a quick overview of common partitioning schemes and file system layouts on Linux servers, along with the equivalent partitions in the Windows world. We will eventually implement a slightly modified version of this scheme for our server.

•   **/**   The root (pronounced *slash* or *root*) partition is identified by a forward slash (/). All other directories are attached (mounted) to this parent directory. It is equivalent to the system drive (**C:\**) in Windows.

•   **/boot**   This partition or volume contains almost everything required for the initial boot process. The equivalent of this in Windows is the system partition (*not* the boot partition).

•   **/boot/efi**   This is the EFI system partition (ESP). This partition (or its equivalent) is mandated by modern systems that implement a Unified Extensible Firmware Interface (UEFI). UEFI is an alternative/replacement for the older Basic Input/Output System (BIOS). UEFI is the very first program that runs when the computer is powered on.

The **/boot/efi** volume is not Linux specific and is thus similarly required on Windows and macOS systems with UEFI. The partition can store boot loaders, kernel images, device drivers, and other utilities.

•   **/usr**   This is where all program files (binaries) commonly reside (similar to **C:\Program Files** in Windows).

•   **/home**   This is where users’ home directories and personal data are stored. Having user data on a separate partition helps to prevent users from inadvertently consuming the entire disk and starving other critical system components that also need storage. This directory is synonymous with **C:\Users\** in Windows operating systems.

•   **/var**   This is where [variable] operating system and application-related data generated during normal system operation is stored. This includes files such as system/event logs, lock files, caches, and mail. Because log files tend to grow in size quickly, it is important to store the logs on a separate partition so that their size or growth is constrained within a defined area. This can help to avoid a type of self-inflicted denial of service attack. Logs are generally stored in the **C:\WINDOWS\system32\config\** directory in Windows.

•   **/tmp**   (Pronounced *slash temp.*) This is where temporary files are placed. Anything stored under the **/tmp** folder is usually not preserved between system reboots. **/tmp** is sometimes implemented as a special virtual memory file system called **tmpfs**.

•   **Swap**   Swap space is an area on the disk that can be used to temporarily offload/extend some of the work done in physical memory (RAM) on a system. It is a type of virtual file system. This isn’t a user-accessible file system. Linux can also use a normal disk file to hold swap space, similar to the way Windows does. Swapping functionality is provided via a paging file in the Windows world.

If the system RAM is less than 4GB, you will typically want to configure your swap file to be double the size of the physical memory that is in your system.

Once defined and created, each of these partitions is mounted at boot time. The mount process makes the contents of that partition available as if it were just another directory on the system. For example, the root directory (**/**) could be on the first partition. A subdirectory called **/usr** will exist on the root directory but will have nothing in it. A separate partition can then be mounted at **/usr**, such that going into the **/usr** directory will allow you to see the contents of the mounted partition or underlying block device. Think of the mount point as a sort of *anchor point*.

Once mounted, all the file systems/partitions/volumes appear as a unified directory tree rather than as separate drives; the installation software does not differentiate one partition from another. All it cares about is which directory each file goes into. As a result, the installation process automatically and correctly distributes its files across all the mounted file systems.

The disk partitioning tool used during the operating system installation provides an easy way to create partitions and associate them to the directories on which they will be mounted. Each mount point entry (or partition entry) will typically show the following information:

•   **Device**   Linux associates each partition with a separate device (file). For the purpose of this installation, you need to know only that entire individual disks are referred to with names that *loosely* follow the pattern **/dev/XYZ**, where:

•   **X** refers to the device type (for example, IDE/SATA/SAS/SCSI/NVMe).

•   **Y** is a letter representing an instance of a unique physical drive of a given type (for example, a, b, c, and so on).

•   **Z** represents a partition number on a given physical drive (for example, 1, 2, 3, and so on).

Let’s apply this pattern to some real-world examples:

•   The first 20TiB SATA SSD disk on a Linux server might be named and addressed as **/dev/sda**.

•   The first partition/slice on the second disk (**/dev/sdb**) will be named and addressed as **/dev/sdb1**.

•   The second partition/slice on the second SATA disk will be named and addressed as **/dev/sdb2**.

•   The first M.2 NVMe PCI-Express Internal SSD detected might be named and addressed as **/dev/nvme0n1**.

•   The fourth partition or slice on the M.2 SSD drive will be named **/dev/nvme0n1p4**.

•   The first virtual hard disk detected or attached to a virtual machine might be named and addressed as **/dev/vda**.

•   **Mount Point**   This field shows the directory location where the partition is mounted.

•   **Desired Capacity**   This field shows the partition’s size in mebibyte (MiB) or gibibyte (GiB).

•   **Device Type**   This field shows the partition type (for example, Standard Partition, BTRFS, LVM, or LVM Thin Provisioning).

•   **File System**   This field shows the partition’s file system type (for example, ext2, ext3, ext4, swap, BIOS Boot, xfs, Btrfs, or vfat).

•   **Reformat**   This field indicates whether the partition will be formatted.

•   **Volume Group**   This field shows the volume group that the partition belongs to. You can either accept the default value or create a new volume group name.

For the sake of simplicity in this chapter, we will accept the default partitioning scheme recommended by the installer. But in a later chapter ([Chapter 8](#ch8.xhtml_ch8)), we will implement some server partitioning and file system layout best practices. This will be done by resizing and/or creating new volumes from scratch using whatever free space we have available on the disk.

The sample UEFI-based system on which this installation is being performed has a 100GB hard disk.

The automatic partitioning tool will by default create the **/boot** partition on a standard partition type. On UEFI-based systems, it will additionally automatically suggest and create a **/boot/efi** partition. It will also automatically create the **/** (root) and swap containers on an LVM-type partition. For more on LVM, see [Chapter 8](#ch8.xhtml_ch8).

The following table shows a summary of the resulting partition/volume sizes and file systems from the automatic partition layout process. You can use this as a guide if you choose to manually carve up your disk yourself. You should, of course, adjust the suggested sizes to suit the overall size of the disk you are using.

![Images](Images/f0027-01.jpg)

Now that you have some background on partitioning under Linux, let’s go back to the installation process itself.

The current unconfigured Manual Partitioning screen (shown previously in [Figure 2-1](#ch2.xhtml_ch2fig1)) presents you with different options. We’ll start by making the installer suggest and automatically create our LVM partitioning scheme for us.

**Automatically Create an LVM Disk Layout**   In the Manual Partitioning screen, make sure that the LVM option is selected under the “New Mount Points will use the following partitioning scheme” drop-down box.

Next, click the “Click here to create them automatically” option.

Choosing the LVM partitioning scheme and allowing the installer to automatically create the mount points, file systems, partitions, and volumes will result in an initial disk layout structure similar to the one shown in the following table.

![Images](Images/f0027-02.jpg)

The exact screen on our sample server is shown next:

![Images](Images/f0028-01.jpg)

**NOTE**  The Fedora installer supports the creation of encrypted file systems; however, we will not use any encrypted file systems on our sample system.

Click Done in the upper-left corner of the Manual Partitioning screen to complete the disk-partitioning portion of the installation. You will be presented with a dialog box showing the summary of changes to be made to the disk.

Click Accept Changes to return to the Installation Summary screen and configure the final option, Network & Hostname.

##### Network & Hostname

The final task of the installation procedure deals with network configuration, where you can configure or tweak network-related settings for the system.

**NOTE**  After you click on the Network & Hostname option, all correctly detected network interface hardware (such as Ethernet, wireless network cards, and so on) will be listed in the left pane of the network configuration screen.

Depending on the Linux distribution and the specific hardware setup, Ethernet devices in Linux have names similar to eth0, eth1, ens3, ens4, em1, em2, p1p1, enp0s3, and so on.

For each interface, you can either configure it using DHCP or manually set the IP address. If you choose to configure manually, be sure to have all the pertinent information ready, such as the IP address, netmask, and so on. Also, don’t worry if you know that you don’t have a DHCP server available on your network that will provide your new system with IP configuration information; the Ethernet interface will simply remain unconfigured. The hostname of the system can also be automatically set via DHCP, if you have a reachable and capable DHCP server on the network.

Clicking the Network & Hostname button in the main Installation Summary screen opens the corresponding configuration screen (see [Figure 2-2](#ch2.xhtml_ch2fig2)). Among other things, you have the option to configure the hostname of the system (the name defaults to **localhost.localdomain**, as shown at the bottom of [Figure 2-2](#ch2.xhtml_ch2fig2)). Note that you can easily change this name later on after the OS has been installed. For now, accept the default value supplied for the hostname.

![Images](Images/F02-02.jpg)

**Figure 2-2**   Network configuration

The next important configuration task is related to the network interfaces on the system. First, verify that an Ethernet card (or any network card) is listed in the left pane. Click any of the detected network devices in the left pane to select it. The configurable properties of the selected network adapter will appear in the right pane of the screen.

On our sample system, we have two Ethernet devices (ens3 and ens10), both of which are in a connected state. The type, name, quantity, and state of the network devices on your system may vary from the ones on our sample system.

After you select a network device, the right pane of the Network & Hostname screen will display the hardware address, speed, IP configuration information (IP address, subnet mask, default route, and DNS) of the device.

Whenever possible, the default behavior is to automatically configure the detected network interface using the Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol (DHCP).

Make sure the switch of the device you want to configure is flipped to the ON position in the right pane.

We will not make any changes on this screen, but if for whatever reason you need to manually specify IP settings for the network device, click the Configure button in the right pane and input your configuration.

Click Done to return to the main Installation Summary screen.

#### User Settings Section

This section can be used for creating a password for the *root* user account and also for creating new administrative or non-administrative accounts.

##### Set the Root Password

Click the Root Password field under User Settings to launch the Root Password task screen. In the Root Password text box, set a strong password for the root user. This user (also called the *superuser)* is the most privileged account on the system and typically has full control of the system. It is equivalent to the administrator account in Windows operating systems. Therefore, it is crucial that you protect this account with a very good password. Be sure not to choose dictionary words or names as passwords, because they are easy to guess and crack.

Enter the same password again in the Confirm text box. Click Done.

##### Create a User Account

Back in the main installation summary screen, click the User Creation field under User Settings to launch the Create User task screen. This task area allows you to create a privileged or non-privileged (non-administrative) user account on the system. Creating and using a non-privileged account for day-to-day tasks on a system is a good system administration practice. You’ll learn how to create additional users manually in [Chapter 6](#ch6.xhtml_ch6). But for now on our sample server, we’ll create a regular user that can invoke superuser (administrator) powers when needed.

Complete the fields in the Create User screen with the following information and then click Done:

![Images](Images/f0031-01.jpg)

#### The Installation

Once you are satisfied with your choices for the various installation tasks, the next phase of the installation process will begin the installation proper.

##### Start the Installation

Once you are satisfied with your choices for the various installation tasks, click the Begin Installation button on the main Installation Summary screen. The installation will begin, and the installer will show the progress of the installation.

**NOTE**  If you develop cold feet after you click the Begin Installation button, you can still safely back out of the installation without any loss of data (or self-esteem). To quit the installer, simply reset your system either by clicking the Quit button, pressing CTRL-ALT-DEL on the keyboard, or pushing the reset or power switch.

When the installation begins, various tasks will begin running in the background, such as partitioning the disk, formatting the partitions or LVM volumes, checking for and resolving software dependencies, writing the operating system to the disk, and so on.

##### Complete the Installation

Once you’ve completed any of the mandatory subtasks and the installer has run its course, complete the installation by clicking the Reboot System button (see [Figure 2-3](#ch2.xhtml_ch2fig3)). The system will reboot itself.

![Images](Images/F02-03.jpg)

**Figure 2-3**   Installation completion

##### Log In

The system is now set up and ready for use. You will see a login screen similar to the one shown here.

![Images](Images/f0031-02.jpg)

To log onto the system, type **master** at the login prompt and press ENTER. At the Password prompt, type **72erty7!2** (master’s password) and press ENTER.

### Installing Ubuntu Server

This section provides a quick overview of installing the Ubuntu Linux distribution in a server configuration. We won’t be as liberal with details as we were for the Fedora server installation, because the same concepts that we discussed in detail earlier carry over here.

First, you need to download the ISO image for the latest Long Term Support (LTS) release of Ubuntu Server (in our example, this is Version 20.04.1 LTS, 64 bit). The ISO image that was used on our sample system was downloaded from [https://ubuntu.com/download/server](https://ubuntu.com/download/server).

We will be performing the installation via flash-based media, such as a USB stick, a Secure Digital (SD) card, or an external hard disk, using the downloaded ISO image. Prior to starting the installation, you need to properly write the downloaded ISO image to the target medium. After writing the ISO image onto the appropriate medium, you should have a bootable Ubuntu Server distribution. [Appendix A](../Text/app1.xhtml) discusses in detail how to create a Linux installer on flash-based media.

Unlike the Fedora installer or the Ubuntu Desktop installer, the Ubuntu Server installer is text-based only and is therefore not quite as pretty.

Complete the following steps to start and complete the installation.

#### Start the Installation

Start the installation as follows:

1.   Insert the Ubuntu Server install media into the proper port on the system.

2.   Make sure the system is set to use the optical drive as its first boot device in the system’s UEFI or BIOS.

3.   Reboot the system if it is currently powered on.

4.   Once the system boots from the install media, you will see an initial boot loader screen with a few menu options. At the boot loader screen shown next, use the ARROW keys on your keyboard to select the Install Ubuntu Server option and then press ENTER.

![Images](Images/f0033-01.jpg)

5.   Select English in the Welcome or preferred language screen and then press ENTER.

6.   Next comes the keyboard configuration section of the installer. On our sample system, we accept the default automatically and correctly detected keyboard layout (English, US) and variant (English, US).

Just in case your keyboard was not correctly automatically detected, you can use the TAB or ARROW keys to navigate to the Identify Keyboard option. Doing this will allow you to manually identify your keyboard layout and variant.

Use the TAB or ARROW keys to navigate to the Done button and then press ENTER.

7.   At the ensuing Welcome to Ubuntu screen, you’ll be presented with a few options for the type of installation you want perform.

Make sure the Install Ubuntu option is highlighted/selected and then press ENTER.

#### Configure the Network

Next comes the network connections portion of the installer.

The installer has correctly detected that our sample server has two network or Ethernet cards (ens3 and ens4). The network cards have also been automatically set up to be configured via DHCP. We can very easily override this default behavior and manually specify the IP settings and other parameters for the cards by highlighting each card and pressing ENTER.

To keep things simple, we accept the default behavior here and use the TAB or ARROW keys to navigate to the Done field and then press ENTER to continue.

#### Configure Proxy

The configure proxy portion of the installation allows you specify the address of a proxy server that the system can use for connecting to the Internet. The address can be specified in the following format:

`http://[user][:pass]@host[:port]/`

Our sample server does not require a proxy server and so we leave the proxy address field blank. Select the Done button and then press ENTER.

#### Configure Ubuntu Archive Mirror

This part of the installer allows you to specify alternative mirrors or archives that the installer can get packages or software from. For example, you might have copies of packages on another server on the local area network that you want to point the installer to.

We are happy with and accept the default mirror address on our sample server.

Select the Done button and then press ENTER.

#### File System Setup

The file system setup screen of the installer that appears allows you to customize the actual partition structure of the system. It is here that you can elect to set up different file systems for different uses (such as **/var**, **/home**, and so on). The same concept used in creating the different partitions during the Fedora installation earlier transfers over for Ubuntu. For the sake of brevity, we will instead accept the default partition and LVM layout recommended by the installer. As a result, we will end up with the following file systems: **/boot**, **/boot/efi**, **/** (root), and **swap**. We are going to use the entire 100GB disk on our demo server and let the installer automatically set it up using LVM.

You’ll have a few options in the current file system setup screen. Use the ARROW keys on your keyboard to select the Use An Entire Disk And Set Up LVM option, as shown here, and then press ENTER.

![Images](Images/f0035-01.jpg)

Another screen will appear, prompting you to select the disk to install to. Accept the default and correctly detected disk and press ENTER.

You’ll next be shown a file system summary screen detailing how the installer will lay out the disk. For our sample server, the summary looks like this:

![Images](Images/f0035-02.jpg)

Use the ARROW keys to select the Done button and then press ENTER.

Due to the real potential for losing any existing data on the target disk, you will be presented with an extra warning/cautionary screen to confirm destructive action. We are installing our demo Ubuntu server on a brand-new and empty disk, so we select the Continue button and press ENTER.

**NOTE**  You might get a different prompt if you are installing the operating system on a disk with existing partitions or volumes. In that case, you will need to confirm that you want to remove any existing partitions or volumes in order to continue.

#### Profile Setup

The next task in the Ubuntu server installation process is to set up a profile. This includes setting up a user account, creating a machine hostname for the server, and so on.

Complete the fields in the ensuing screen with the following information:

1.   In the Your Name field, type in the full name **master admin**. Use the TAB or ENTER key to change to the next field.

2.   Type **ubuntu-server** in the Your server’s name field. Use the TAB or ENTER key to change to the next field.

3.   Type **master** in the Pick a username field. Use the TAB or ENTER key to change to the next field.

4.   Enter the password **72erty7!2** in the Choose a password field. Use the TAB or ENTER key to change to the next field.

5.   Retype the same password in the Confirm your password field. Use the TAB or ARROW keys to select the Done button.

6.   Press ENTER when the Done button is selected/highlighted

#### SSH Setup

The next task in the installation process is to install an OpenSSH server, import relevant SSH keys, and complete some minimal OpenSSH configuration tasks. A running OpenSSH server is useful for remotely accessing and managing systems and so we’ll go ahead and install it here.

1.   Use the TAB or ARROW keys to navigate to the Install OpenSSH server field.

2.   Use the SPACE bar or ENTER keys on your keyboard to select/enable or put a check-mark on the Install OpenSSH server option.

3.   We will not be importing any SSH keys or Usernames at this time. Accept the default setting (No) in the Import SSH identity and Username fields.

4.   Accept any other remaining configuration defaults in the SSH Setup screen

5.   Use the TAB or ARROW keys to select the final Done button.

6.   Press ENTER when the Done button is selected/highlighted.

#### Featured Server Snaps

The concept of *snaps* in the Ubuntu server world is a different implementation of preconfigured package groups, add-ons, modules, or software collections than in the Fedora/RedHat/CentOS world. Snaps provide a specific functionality and are self-contained file systems, apps, libraries, and so on.

We will not be installing any snaps at this time on our demo Ubuntu server. Use the TAB or ARROW keys to select Done and then press ENTER.

#### Install Complete

If you blink your eyes, you’ll miss it—the installation will be done!

Select the Reboot button and press ENTER. You might be prompted to remove the installation media (flash drive, SD card, optical media, and so on) and then press ENTER.

Once the system reboots, you will be presented with a simple login prompt (see [Figure 2-4](#ch2.xhtml_ch2fig4)). You can log in as the user that was previously created during the installation. The username is **master** and the password is **72erty7!2**.

![Images](Images/F02-04.jpg)

**Figure 2-4**   Classic Ubuntu Linux login prompt

### Summary

You have successfully completed the installation process. If you are having problems with the installation, be sure to visit Fedora’s web site at [https://getfedora.org](https://getfedora.org) or the Ubuntu web site at [www.ubuntu.com](http://www.ubuntu.com) and take a look at the various manuals and tips available.

The version release notes are also a good resource for specific installation issues. Even though the install process discussed in this chapter used Fedora and Ubuntu as the operating systems of choice, you can rest assured that the installation concepts for other Linux distributions are virtually identical.

We sprinkled (and discussed) a liberal amount of GNU Linux/FOSS-specific concepts (for example, hard disk naming conventions, partitioning, volume management, network configuration, software management, and so on) throughout our installation walkthrough. These concepts will be covered in more detail in later chapters.

### 3

 |  
### Deploying Linux Servers in the Cloud

 |

With the prevalence of cloud providers today, it’s more feasible and easier than ever for everybody to launch and run their own Linux servers. End users have a wide variety of providers and implementations to select from, such as OpenStack, Linode, Amazon Web Services (AWS), Google Cloud Platform (GCP), Azure, and IBM Cloud.

The speed and ease with which a brand-new Linux server distribution can be brought online almost makes the hard work we put into [Chapter 2](#ch2.xhtml_ch2) seem like a waste! Almost everything comes prebaked for you in the cloud. You only need to know how to turn on or off the right switches to get up and running in the cloud—and have the appropriate billing information handy, of course. With this in mind, you can view this chapter as an alternate Linux server installation chapter—but without any actual installation!

### Behind the Cloud

Cloud environments are powered by a gazillion virtual machines (VMs). VMs are powered by the operating system (OS). The OS is powered by hardware or physical machines—loads and loads of hardware. You can rest assured there are no magical unicorns making things happen in the cloud. Cloud environments are powered by hardware.

What this means for you as a Linux system administrator is that *more than ever,* your skills and knowledge are heavily needed—even in a cloud-driven world. So instead of thinking in terms of a few physical hard drives attached to servers, you now think in terms of petabytes and pools of storage to be shared by potentially hundreds of smaller VMS. Instead of thinking in terms of terabytes of installed physical memory (RAM), you now think in terms of splitting that memory into smaller sizes to be shared by lots of smaller virtual machines (or containers). Instead of thinking in terms of a couple of Ethernet cards on a box, you think in terms of hundreds of virtual network cards and switches all communicating using the magic of software-defined networking (SDN). In a nutshell, this all means that the work (and concerns) of a system administrator increases by orders of magnitude in a cloud environment!

### Obtaining and Spinning Up New Virtual Linux Servers

In this section, we talk about some of the many quick methods for spinning up a new Linux server—but using other people’s hardware and infrastructure! Once it is successfully spun up, you should be able to apply the theories and follow the exercises in the rest of the book, just as if you were following along on your own physical machine.

Because we’ve not yet covered some other pertinent details (such as working on the command line), our coverage here is necessarily going to be very high level. The virtualization chapter later on delves deeper into this topic. At a minimum, you will need access to the command-line interface of an existing system (preferably Linux), with the right tools installed, in order to be able to use the commands detailed in the next sections. Even though we prefer Linux-based systems, you won’t be stranded if you are following along on another platform such as macOS or Windows—you’ll just have to consult the relevant provider documentation for how to obtain and set up the tools on either of those platforms.

#### Free-to-Run Virtual Linux Servers

By “free-to-run,” we mean you don’t necessarily need to give your billing information or credit card details to any third-party provider to get a virtual Linux server up and running. As a result, this often involves some hands-on prep work to be done by you or somebody else! We only provide a few examples of this type of server in this section.

##### virt-builder

This is a utility for downloading or building new virtual machines via customizable templates. It is easy to use, and all you need is access to an existing, running Linux operating system. The authors of **virt-builder** have created a decent library of templates for building various versions and spins of popular Linux distributions, such as Fedora, Ubuntu, Debian, OpenSUSE, and CentOS. After installing the software package that provides the **virt-builder** utility, you can use it to query and view a list of available operating systems by running the following command:

![Images](Images/f0040-01.jpg)

To view any relevant installation notes (such as login passwords, usernames, and so on) that might be available for the fedora-34 distro returned in the preceding sample listing, type this command:

`$` **`virt-builder --notes fedora-34`**

Next, run the following command to build and download the disk image file for our sample fedora-34 distro. By default, the file will be downloaded to the current working directory.

`$` **`virt-builder fedora-34`**

After successfully downloading the raw virtual disk image file (fedora34.img in our example), you should be able to use any garden-variety hypervisor platform to boot up and run the VM encapsulated in the image file. [Chapter 30](#ch30.xhtml_ch30) covers how to use the **virt-install** utility to import and run disk images on the native Linux Kernel hypervisor (KVM).

##### OpenStack

OpenStack is an amalgamation of several individual FOSS projects that can be integrated to provide a single and complete cloud computing platform suitable for public and private clouds. Collectively, the individual projects are responsible for powering some very important services that OpenStack relies heavily on, such as Compute (Nova), Networking (Neutron), Block Storage (Cinder), Identity (Keystone), Image (Glance), Object Storage (Swift), Database (Trove), and Messaging (Zaqar). The OpenStack project has the backing of lots of technology industry stalwarts that use the project as well as contribute to its development. Once OpenStack is properly set up and configured, you are limited only by your imagination for what you can do with it.

Although the individual projects that comprise OpenStack usually have their own native tools (and quirks), the overarching **openstack** binary aims to be a unified tool that can be used to perform numerous functions across the entire stack. You can learn more about and download the **openstack** client toolset from [https://pypi.org/project/python-openstackclient/](https://pypi.org/project/python-openstackclient/).

After configuring and authorizing the tool to work on the target **openstack** deployment, you can bring up a new Linux server VM by supplying the correct parameters and running the following:

![Images](Images/f0041-02.jpg)

#### Commercial Cloud Service Providers

Commercial cloud providers are any of the many for-profit companies that rent out parts of their compute infrastructure for a fee. Even though most of these providers have so-called free tiers of their services, you can rest assure that there is no such thing as a completely free lunch. The free tiers are designed to wet your appetite just enough to get you addicted/hooked on their services. Most commercial service providers require you to sign up and establish security tokens and keys that are unique to that service or provider. Generally, to use the command-line interface (CLI) tools in the following sections, you need to have security tokens handy!

**Application Programming Interface (API)**

One phrase you’ll come across very frequently in the cloud world is application programming interface, or API. Here, we explain how APIs came to be and what problems they solve.

When you are running your workloads in the cloud, you are relying on the cloud provider’s physical infrastructure. This means that you don’t have access to physical switches, buttons, cables, ports, or anything like you would have in your own server closet or data center. The only way to manage your environment is via whatever virtual (software) interfaces the provider makes available to you. The interface of choice that most providers make available is via an API. APIs can be crudely defined as a canned set of rules designed to complete or trigger certain functions that a provider makes available to authorized users. For example, a provider can have a set of APIs that end users can invoke to launch a brand-new Fedora server VM with 128GB of RAM in a data center located in Antarctica. APIs can help provide a software abstraction layer that end users can interact with in a controlled manner.

The net result of all this is that OpenStack, Google, AWS, Azure, Bob, and his uncle all have their own unique APIs that you must use to interact with them. Thankfully, most of the APIs are implemented via a common and well-understood Representational State Transfer (REST) interface. Once you are authorized and understand the nuances of a system’s API, you can easily bring up a single or a thousand new Linux servers using a few well-crafted commands!

##### Linode

Linode has a long and rich history in the Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS) world, specifically in the area of its Linux-based distro offerings. A VM in the Linode world is often referred to as a “linode” (Linux node).

Besides the graphical web front-end for managing resources in the Linode cloud, end users also have the option of a rich command line interface aptly named Linode CLI. The Linode CLI is a wrapper around the rich Linode API. You can download and learn more about Linode CLI from [https://github.com/linode/linode-cli](https://github.com/linode/linode-cli).

Once it’s properly configured and you supply the correct parameters, you should be able to bring up a sample linode VM under your account with a command similar to the one here:

![Images](Images/f0042-01.jpg)

##### Amazon Web Services (AWS)

AWS provides cloud computing services and products for various applications and industries. There are literarily hundreds of services under the AWS umbrella. Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (EC2) is the specific AWS offering that provides the compute infrastructure that interests us here.

AWS and numerous third parties have curated a decent collection of virtual machines on the EC2 platform. The AWS homegrown tool for interacting with its various cloud services is called **aws** or **aws-cli**. You can learn more about the aws tool at [https://aws.amazon.com/cli/](https://aws.amazon.com/cli/).

After signing up for an AWS account and properly configuring the tool, you can launch a new VM in AWS by supplying the correct values for the parameters (Amazon Machine Image ID, number of instances, and so on) in the following sample command:

![Images](Images/f0043-01.jpg)

##### Google Cloud Platform (GCP)

GCP is made up of a plethora of services—and the number of services keeps growing. The specific component under GCP that is closest to offering a traditional Linux (virtual) server experience to end users is the Google Compute Engine (GCE). Google’s homegrown command-line toolset for end users to interact with its products and service under GCP is delivered via its Cloud SDK. The specific tool for interacting with GCE is called **gcloud**. You can download and learn more about the Cloud SDK and **gcloud** at [https://cloud.google.com/sdk/](https://cloud.google.com/sdk/).

After signing up for a GCP account and setting up your environment, bringing up a new Linux server can be as simple as supplying the correct values for the parameters (image family, image project, and so on) and running the following command:

![Images](Images/f0043-02.jpg)

##### Azure

Azure is Microsoft’s cloud computing arm. As of the time of this writing, it comprises over several hundred different cloud services! The Azure component we are interested in here is aptly name “Virtual Machines,” and it allows end users to create Linux and Windows virtual machines on Azure’s IaaS platform.

Azure CLI (**az**) is the command-line tool for managing various things in the Azure world. You can download and learn more about this tool at [https://github.com/Azure/azure-cli](https://github.com/Azure/azure-cli).

As with the other commercial public cloud providers, you’ll need to sign up for an account before you can start spinning up servers on Azure’s infrastructure. Once you have the **az** tool properly set up and you’ve created any needed resources (such as a resource group), you should be able to spin up a sample Ubuntu server in Azure by running a command similar to the one here:

![Images](Images/f0043-03.jpg)

### Summary

Even though almost everything in the cloud is virtual, it is still very important that you as the system administrator have a good understanding of the main principles of administering physical servers. The concepts are very similar; only the scale is different. The rest of this book covers a good chunk of the main principles of Linux server administration, such that you will be ready to work on both physical and virtual cloud-based servers.

As we wrote at the beginning of this chapter, one of the beauties of the cloud computing model is that almost everything comes prebaked for you in the cloud. However, to take full advantage of the ease of use and accessibility of the cloud, you need to be able to speak the language of the provider and play by their rules—and this is often done via APIs and custom tools wrapped around the APIs. [Chapter 30](#ch30.xhtml_ch30) provides more insight into the world of virtualization on which all cloud environments are built.

### 4
